recluse

REK-loos -- from Latin reclusus, 're- (back) + claudere (to close)': a recluse has closed themself off from the world. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Recluse is a person who lives a solitary, withdrawn life, avoiding others.

The author of the famous novel turned out to be a recluse who had given exactly one interview in forty years.

Example

Once famous for climbing the tallest peaks on every continent, the retired mountaineer became a recluse: he stopped answering letters, moved to a remote valley, and was not seen by another person for nearly a year.

A recluse withdraws almost entirely from other people -- the mountaineer's fame makes the contrast especially striking, since someone once so publicly admired chose complete isolation instead.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

introvert: An introvert recharges through quiet and enjoys company in smaller doses, but still keeps friends and a full life. A recluse actually withdraws from society, cutting off most human contact. Being an introvert is a personality style; becoming a recluse is a way of life.

shut-in: A shut-in stays home because illness or frailty makes leaving hard, and the word points squarely at that physical confinement. Recluse is broader: a recluse may withdraw by choice or by circumstance, and the word describes avoiding people, not being unable to reach them.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

socialite: a person who is very active in fashionable social life

extrovert: an outgoing, sociable person

Where it sits · how complete the withdrawal is — loner → recluse → hermit

loner vs. recluse: Loner is a common, everyday word for someone who simply prefers solitude, while recluse suggests a more complete, often extreme withdrawal from society.

hermit vs. recluse: Hermit goes further than recluse, often carrying an image of total isolation in a remote place, sometimes for religious or spiritual reasons.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back, away (Latin)

root — -cluse

root — -cluse: to close, shut (Latin claudere)

Put it together

Put it together: Recluse comes from Latin reclusus, the past participle of recludere, 're- (back) + claudere (to close)' -- a recluse has, in effect, shut themself away from the world, the same root behind the word exclude.

Use the root in a new word: exclude

Use the root in a new word: exclude: The new rule excludes anyone under sixteen from entering the arcade after nine at night.
